vignette:
He is 19 now, a North American young man who works the evening shift at a fast-food restaurant, but he still measures time by the storm that tore through his neighborhood. Before that night, his life feels ordinary in the way adolescence often does: school, friends, shifting plans, and long hours on his feet at work where the smell of hot oil clings to his uniform even after he gets home. He is single and keeps mostly to himself, with a small circle of people he trusts. Since the disaster, he says, ordinary life has not felt as simple or predictable.

The storm hits hard and without warning in the middle of the night. He is in bed when the wind begins to sound wrong, like something large moving too close to the house. Then come the crashes, the sharp banging of debris, the shuddering walls, and the power going out all at once. He remembers the dark most clearly. It is complete and immediate, and in it he cannot tell what is outside and what is already inside. He hears his family shouting over the noise, and he feels a kind of helplessness he had never known before. There is water coming in, branches striking the siding, and a roof section that gives way with a sound he later describes as "like the house was splitting open." He spends much of that night frozen in place, waiting for the worst thing to happen.

In the days after, he moves through the cleanup in a stunned state. The neighborhood looks unfamiliar: downed trees, broken fences, rooftops torn away, power lines sagging, the smell of wet insulation and mud hanging in the air. He helps where he can, but mostly he keeps scanning the sky. Even when the weather is clear, he cannot relax. Any sudden change in wind, any dark cloud, pulls him back into that night. He starts sleeping lightly, waking to small sounds, checking his phone for weather alerts before he can fully get out of bed. He tells himself he is just being careful, but the carefulness becomes constant.

At work, he tries to act normal. The restaurant is loud, bright, and busy, and the routine should be grounding, but instead it sometimes feels like too much noise, too much movement, too many demands at once. When the fryer sputters or metal pans slam, he jolts before he can stop himself. He notices his body reacting first and his thoughts catching up afterward. He becomes frustrated with himself for flinching, for losing track of orders, for needing to step into the back room when storm clouds gather. He does not want coworkers to see how easily he gets rattled. He keeps his head down, speaks less, and takes extra shifts when he can, partly for money and partly because staying busy seems safer than being alone with his thoughts.

The memories do not stay where he wants them. They come in flashes: the sound of the roof cracking, the look on his family's faces, the wet cold of that night. Sometimes he finds himself suddenly back there, not in a full vision but in a body memory-a tight chest, clenched jaw, and the sense that he needs to move now. He avoids anything that reminds him too much of the storm. He does not watch weather coverage, does not like thunder, and does not want to drive past the damaged houses in his old neighborhood. He notices himself taking a longer route home if the horizon looks unsettled.

Over time, his world narrows. He still goes to work and keeps up appearances, but he feels less interested in hanging out, less able to enjoy things that used to pass the time. He is quicker to irritation and slower to calm. When people ask how he is doing, he gives short answers and changes the subject. At night, he lies awake replaying what happened and imagining what would have happened if the storm had hit a little differently. He tells himself he should be over it by now, yet his body continues to act as if danger is close. Even in the present, he carries the storm with him, listening for it in every sudden gust, every warning tone, every change in the air.
